lead: Prestressing works only if the two materials pull their weight. The concrete must carry a large permanent compression without crushing or splitting, and the steel must hold a high tensile stress without yielding. That is why prestressed concrete uses high-strength concrete of grade M40 and above together with high-tensile steel in the form of wires, strands or bars. The pair makes long spans, thin sections and crack-free service possible in bridges, water tanks and railway sleepers.
prereq: You need Unit 1 on stress-strain behaviour of concrete and steel, and 6.1 for why prestress keeps concrete in compression.

blocks.text: A tendon of area A<sub>p</sub> stressed to f<sub>p</sub> applies a force P = A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>p</sub> to the concrete. Here A<sub>p</sub> is the tendon area in mm² and f<sub>p</sub> is the tensile stress in the steel in N/mm². P is in newtons when the units are mm² and N/mm². Prestressing forces are large, often hundreds of kilonewtons.

Ordinary mild steel yields at about 250 N/mm². A tendon at that stress would need a huge area to give the same force, so the section becomes heavy and uneconomical. High-tensile steel carries 1500 N/mm² or more, so a small tendon gives a large force. High-strength concrete then carries the resulting compression, bond and bearing stresses.

blocks.where: P is the prestressing force in N; A<sub>p</sub> is the tendon cross-section area in mm²; f<sub>p</sub> is the tensile stress in the tendon in N/mm².

blocks.text: Concrete grade M40 means a characteristic cube compressive strength of 40 N/mm² at 28 days. The test uses 150 mm cubes. Prestressed work commonly starts at M40 and goes higher; a few codes allow M30 for lightly stressed members, but the trend is strong concrete.

High strength comes from a low water-cement ratio, good grading, adequate cement and careful compaction and curing. The tensile strength also rises with grade, but it remains a small fraction of the cube strength. Concrete is still weak in tension, so prestress must keep tensile stresses low or absent.

blocks.where: E<sub>c</sub> is the modulus of elasticity of concrete in N/mm²; f<sub>ck</sub> is the characteristic cube compressive strength in N/mm².

blocks.text: For M40, E<sub>c</sub> ≈ 5000√40 ≈ 31,600 N/mm². A stiffer concrete deflects less and holds the tendon force with less shortening. Higher strength also gives better resistance to creep and shrinkage, which reduces losses later.

Bearing and bond govern many details. At an anchorage, the jack force enters through a small plate, so local bearing stress is high. In pre-tensioning, the force transfers from steel to concrete by bond over a short transmission length. Strong concrete resists splitting, crushing and slip in both cases. See 6.7 for end-block design.

High-tensile steel comes as wire, strand or bar. A wire is a single small-diameter product, plain or indented. A strand is a group of wires twisted together. The common 7-wire strand has one central wire and six outer wires wound helically around it. A bar is a solid alloy-steel product, sometimes threaded for anchorage. Wires and strands commonly reach 1500 to 1900 N/mm²; bars are usually lower.

The stress-strain curve has no clear yield plateau. It is nearly straight at working stress, then bends gradually, reaches a peak and fails at a small strain. There is no yield point like mild steel. Design therefore uses the 0.1% proof stress f<sub>p0.1</sub>: draw a line parallel to the linear part, offset by 0.1% strain, and read the stress where it meets the curve. This is the stress that leaves a permanent strain of 0.1% after unloading.

For a typical strand, the 0.1% proof stress is about 85 to 90 percent of the ultimate tensile strength f<sub>pu</sub>. f<sub>pu</sub> is the maximum stress on the stress-strain curve. A designer checks the tendon stress against the proof stress, not against 250 N/mm², and not against the ultimate strength without a material factor.

Relaxation is another property of high-tensile steel. When a tendon is held at constant length, its stress slowly falls with time. This is relaxation, not creep: creep is strain change under constant stress; relaxation is stress change under constant strain. Low-relaxation strands reduce this loss. The calculation belongs to 6.5.

figure.caption: Prestressing needs both layers: concrete strong enough for M40 and above, and steel strong enough to carry high tensile stress.

spec.aria: Two material layers: high-strength concrete grade M40 and above, and high-tensile steel in wires, strands and bars.

examples.question: A pre-tensioned tendon has cross-section area A<sub>p</sub> = 100 mm² and is stressed to f<sub>p</sub> = 1600 N/mm². (a) Find the prestressing force P. (b) Find the area of mild steel needed to carry the same force at a permissible stress of 250 N/mm². (c) State one practical conclusion.
steps: For mild steel, A<sub>s</sub> = P / f<sub>s</sub> = 160,000 N / 250 N/mm² = 640 mm².
The high-tensile tendon needs 100 mm², while mild steel needs 640 mm² for the same force.
examples.answer: The prestressing force is 160 kN, and the equivalent mild-steel area is 640 mm².
examples.check:
Ap = 100.0
fp = 1600.0
P = Ap * fp
print(int(P))
print(int(P / 1000))
print(int(P / 250))

traps: Using 250 N/mm² as the design strength of high-tensile steel. It has no clear yield point; use the 0.1% proof stress.
Reading M40 as 40 N/mm² tensile strength. M40 is characteristic cube compressive strength.
Mixing units: mm² × N/mm² gives N, not kN. Divide by 1000 only at the end.
Saying high-tensile steel is ductile because it is strong. It has low elongation and fails with little warning.
Confusing relaxation with creep. Relaxation is stress loss at constant strain; creep is strain growth at constant stress.

quiz.q: What does grade M40 mean for concrete?
quiz.a: Characteristic cube compressive strength of 40 N/mm² at 28 days, tested on 150 mm cubes.

quiz.q: Name the three common forms of high-tensile prestressing steel.
Why does an anchorage zone need high-strength concrete?
quiz.a: The jack force enters through a small bearing plate, causing high local bearing and splitting stresses; strong concrete resists crushing and splitting.

quiz.q: Why is 0.1% proof stress used for high-tensile steel?
quiz.a: The steel has no clear yield point, so design uses the stress at which unloading leaves a permanent strain of 0.1%.

quiz.q: A tendon has A<sub>p</sub> = 150 mm² and f<sub>p</sub> = 1500 N/mm². Find P in kN.
Compare mild steel at 250 N/mm² with high-tensile steel at 1600 N/mm² for a force of 200 kN.
quiz.a: Mild steel area = 200,000 / 250 = 800 mm²; high-tensile area = 200,000 / 1600 = 125 mm². High-tensile steel saves 675 mm², about 84%.

quiz.q: Give two reasons a 7-wire strand is preferred to one large wire of the same area.
quiz.a: It is more flexible for handling and curving; the helical outer wires improve bond; standard anchors grip strands well.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern prestressed concrete often uses low-relaxation 7-wire strand with ultimate strength around 1860 N/mm². Ultra-high-performance concrete, with compressive strengths well above 150 N/mm², is used in special footbridges and precast elements. Corrosion protection by galvanizing, epoxy coating or grouting is a major field. Search next for low-relaxation strand, transmission length, and anchorage bearing stress.
